{{Use American English|date=January 2019}}{{Short description|Theorem of quantum circuits}}In [[quantum computing]], the '''Gottesman&ndash;Knill theorem''' is a theoretical result by [[Daniel Gottesman]] and [[Emanuel Knill]] that states that stabilizer circuits&mdash;circuits that only consist of gates from the [[Centralizer and normalizer|normalizer]] of the qubit [[Pauli group]], also called [[Clifford gates|Clifford group]]&mdash;can be perfectly simulated in polynomial time on a probabilistic classical computer. The Clifford group can be [[Generating set of a group|generated]] solely by using the [[controlled NOT gate|controlled NOT]], [[Hadamard gate|Hadamard]], and phase gates (CNOT, ''H'' and ''S'');<ref name="aaronson2004improved">{{cite journal
 | first1 = Scott  
 | last1 = Aaronson
 | first2 = Daniel
 | last2 = Gottesman
 | author-link1 = Scott Aaronson
 | author-link2 = Daniel Gottesman
 | journal =  Physical Review A
 | volume = 70
 | number = 5
 | article-number = 052328
 | year = 2004
 | title = Improved simulation of stabilizer circuits
 | arxiv = quant-ph/0406196
 | doi=10.1103/physreva.70.052328
| bibcode = 2004PhRvA..70e2328A
 | s2cid = 5289248
 }}</ref> and therefore [[Group action (mathematics)|stabilizer]] circuits can be constructed using only these gates. 

The reason for the speed up of quantum computers compared to classical ones is not yet fully understood{{Citation needed|date=October 2020}}. The Gottesman-Knill theorem proves that all quantum algorithms whose speed up relies on entanglement that can be achieved with [[Controlled NOT gate|CNOT]] and [[Hadamard]] gates do not achieve any computational advantage relative to classical computers, due to the classical simulability of such algorithms (and the particular types of entangled states they can produce). 

Since the theorem's initial statement, more efficient constructions for simulating such stabilizer (Clifford) circuits have been identified<ref name="aaronson2004improved"></ref> with an implementation.<ref name="https://www.scottaaronson.com/chp/">{{cite web|last1=Aaronson|first1=Scott|last2=Gottesman|first2=Daniel|author-link1=Scott Aaronson|author-link2=Daniel Gottesman|title=CHP: CNOT-Hadamard-Phase|url=https://www.scottaaronson.com/chp/|website=scottaaronson|access-date=19 September 2017}}</ref>

The Gottesman&ndash;Knill theorem was published in a single-author paper by [[Daniel Gottesman|Gottesman]], in which he credits [[Emanuel Knill|Knill]] with the result, through private communication.<ref>{{cite arXiv
 | last = Gottesman
 | first = Daniel
 | author-link = Daniel Gottesman
 | year = 1998
 | title = The Heisenberg Representation of Quantum Computers
 | eprint = quant-ph/9807006
}}</ref>

== Formal statement==
Theorem:  A quantum circuit using only the following elements can be simulated efficiently on a classical computer:
# Preparation of [[qubit]]s in computational-basis states.
# [[Clifford gates]] (generated by the [[Hadamard gate]], [[controlled NOT gate]], and phase gate ''S'' ).
# Measurements in the computational basis.

The Gottesman&ndash;Knill theorem shows that even some highly [[Quantum entanglement|entangled]] states can be simulated efficiently on a classical computer. Several important types of quantum algorithms use only Clifford gates, including the standard algorithms for [[entanglement distillation]] and [[quantum error correction]]. From a practical point of view, stabilizer circuits on ''n'' qubits can be simulated in {{math|''O''(''n''&nbsp;log&nbsp;''n'')}} time using the [[graph state]] formalism.
